utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution takes the position that this witness has previously been granted protective measures, including facial distortion, based on the 27 February 2001 order of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So be it, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have a document with identifying information about the witness. I'd ask the usher to show one copy of that to the witness and distribute the remaining copies, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you can have a seat. And for the record, I believe this is Witness I, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please take a look at the document that's been provided to you and verify that your name and date of birth are correctly stated on that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that this document be marked as the next exhibit in order, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the first few questions, I'd ask that we go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please briefly describe for the Court the deterioration of relations between the Bosniak Muslims and the Serbs in opstina Prijedor in the late 1980s, early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: After the breakdown of the communist party and the central committee, new parties were established, the democratic parties, which in each own territories conducted their activities and in their own republic of the then Yugoslavia, then the elections came and the power was shared proportionately to the vote that was won. In Bosnia we had three strong parties, the SDA, HDZ and SDS and this is how it was supposed to stay, the power to be shared and the situation to be stabilised but some republics demanded secession and independence. Bosnia did so, and opted for a prosperous sovereign state and at that point, the tensions developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with some Bosnian Muslims and some Bosnian Croats who, in fact, did go to the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon their return to Bosnia following that war, what happened to their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The reservists who were ethnic Croats and Bosniaks who came back from Croatia had their weapons taken away from them whereas the ethnic Serbs who came back were allowed to take their weapons home with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with a plebescite that occurred in Bosnia in February 1992 and, if so, can you please describe that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS held a plebescite of the Serb people, and only Serbs could participate in it. The question asked was whether they wanted to stay within Yugoslavia. This is how it was formulated so there was no other options, only the question that was asked. And in this plebescite, it was decided, apparently, that they would live in one state, that they would establish a state which would be part -- which would then be together with Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following this plebescite, was there a further referendum that was held in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, there was a referendum of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was public, open to all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the independence and separate Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what the results of that referendum were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The result of the referendum was positive. Many states had already recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina on the basis of this referendum. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the ethnic groups in Bosnia boycott the election or the referendum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb side boycotted the referendum. They did not want to come out to vote in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, shortly after the referendum, did there come a time when the SDS took over power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. One day - it was in April, late March, early April - the Serb authorities, that is, the SDS party, ordered the ethnic Serb policemen to disarm their own fellow policemen who were of Croat or Bosniak ethnic background and send them home, and this is how the power was taken over in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe -- at this approximate time, can you describe any changes that occurred to the media in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The Kozarski Vjesnik was no longer Kozarski Vjesnik but Srpski Kozarski Vjesnik. The Radio Prijedor became the Radio Serb Prijedor. So they had their media, and we had no newspapers or any other media outlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time were you able to receive radio and television broadcasts from Zagreb or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. For another period of time, we were able to get Sarajevo broadcasts and a few people could also get the Zagreb broadcasts, but then the television relay was -- on Mount Kozara was taken over, and from that day on, we were no longer able to view anything else but the programming from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time period when that occurred, when you were only able to get broadcasts from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, once the police had been taken over by the Serbs, did you notice any visible changes in the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. They automatically changed the insignia on their uniforms. They started wearing the tricolour, red, quite, and blue. No five-pointed star but the four-S symbol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At approximately the same time, were the flags changed over all government buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, prior to the takeover, would it be fair to say that you frequently went into the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about after the takeover? Did you still continue to go into the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: From my place to downtown Prijedor, there were three or four checkpoints which one had to pass and show identity cards, some kind of identification document. One would be automatically stopped or turned back. So we didn't even want to try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did people in your village possess hunting weapons of any kind prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those weapons once the war started in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The hunting weapons and personal weapons which some citizens possessed had to be turned in by 12.00 - this was an ultimatum - and if not, they said that they would shell us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when there was a specific ultimatum Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 directed at your village of Donja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That was the ultimatum, to surrender weapons until 12.00 and to sign an oath of loyalty to the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date when that ultimatum was issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That would have been around 24 -- between 24 to 28th of May. I'm not certain of the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a part of this ultimatum, were the villagers in Donja Ljubija asked to turn anyone over to the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They did not demand in Donja Ljubija, but in other villages, the villages that were before my village, they demanded that Aziz Aliskovic be surrendered, which they didn't do, and they started shelling that area Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Biscani, Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you required to make any outward demonstrations of loyalty to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. The inhabitants of my village were supposed to hoist white flags outside of their homes, and the police station in Ljubija, that is, its personnel had to sign an oath of loyalty to the Serb authorities and the Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a person by the name of Aziz Aliskovic. Did you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him before the war. That was a policeman who worked in Ljubija for many years. For a period he also worked in Prijedor. I knew him not quite as a friend but as a good acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did there then come a time when your village, Donja Ljubija, was taken over by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. The police station in Gornja Ljubija was taken over, and a Serb police was established. The ultimatum that they had issued us was implemented. We turned in the weapons, and so this was the situation that took place for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of fighting or armed conflict in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, not in Ljubija. There was no fighting in Ljubija. There was no resistance. Not a single shot was fired from our side, that is, the side of the Croats and Bosniaks. So for a while, there was a period of calm, of a lull.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Serb troops entered the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall the exact date, but one morning, from the direction of Brdo, Hegici, and Bradina, a lot of soldiers, a lot of troops poured in with -- wearing various uniforms, some bandannas, leather gloves and all kinds of paraphernalia. They started rounding up men and women. They started pulling jewellery off of women. They were asking for money. They were asking for valuables. And then at the same time from the direction of Ljeskari, a tank arrived accompanied by a JNA unit, that is the newly reconfigured JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there a mosque in your village prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. There was a mosque and an orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the mosque once the Serbs arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, they entered the mosque. They set the rugs on fire. They found a religious flag which they brought out. They put it on the tank. They drove about with that flag on top of the tank. They entered the SDA offices in Ljubija. They ransacked it. They smashed the office. They found a picture of Josip Broz Tito. They hung it on a linden tree and used it for target practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when the Serb troops -- immediately after the Serb troops entered your village, were any of the villagers harmed or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. In the attack on the village, Smajo Ikanovic was killed. About 500 men were taken to the stadium at Gornja Ljubija, that was half of my village. That is the one to the railroad tracks on the side of the Hegici, Hasanagici, and Gradina, that is how far this attack went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you one of the men that was taken to the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I was lucky. I crossed the railroad tracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the other half was driven by fear. Everybody was abandoning their houses. Everybody had heard about men being taken to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: [redacted]. We were about perhaps 70 men. We were hiding in woods perhaps 100 metres away from my home. We had abandoned our homes, our mothers, wives, all out of fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were any of the men that were with you hiding in the woods behind your house armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. We had turned over our weapons about ten days previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, or have you heard from others what happened to the men that were taken to the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, the men who were taken to the stadium were slapped, some of them, interrogated, some of them. I don't know really. Sometime in the afternoon towards the evening, they were released. Someone from the police station of Ljubija reacted and let these men go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, while you were -- when you fled into the hills, where was your wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: My wife, my mother, and my one-year-old child were at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your wife was pregnant at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: My wife was pregnant before the attack on Hambarine. At that time, she had already returned from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to her at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Before the attack on Hambarine, I have just said that [redacted] [redacted]. And from the side of that Serbian hamlet, there was fire from a machine-gun, from a light machine-gun, and my wife was seven months pregnant at the time. Her water broke. That was on the 21st of May. We called an ambulance, and she went to Prijedor to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to her at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: She stayed at the hospital for about seven days without getting any medical assistance or care. They did absolutely nothing to help her deliver as soon as possible. Seven days later, they put her in an ambulance and drove her to Banja Luka and at that moment, Kozarac had already been set on fire and destroyed, and she passed through the destroyed Kozarac. She stayed for about 15 days in Banja Luka and gave birth there. The child was still alive when it was born. It cried. It was a boy, but nothing was done for him. He was not put in an ICU, and it died. We know nothing of its fate. We don't know whether it was buried or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, immediately after the attack on your village, did you then return from the hills to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately in the evening, we went back home. When we heard that the men from the stadium had returned, we returned as well. And from that day on, peace reigned for another ten days, and then the Serbian police came. They went from house to house and started arresting men and taking them to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during this period, Witness, when you were interrogated by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the conditions under which you were interrogated and approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, in the period while my wife was in the hospital - and from day one I didn't know where she was and what was happening to her - I got a message that I had to report to the Ljubija police station. I complied. I was interrogated up there by the then commander, Branko Bjekic. I seem to remember that was his name. He was of Croatian ethnicity. He was commander before the takeover, and on paper at least, he remained commander even after the take-over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall any of the other police officers who were present at any time while you were being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: And the actual commander was actually Savo Pusac. I went to a separate office to give my statement. The statement was taken by policeman Daljevic, whose first name I don't know, and Mr. Drago Tokmadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how many times were you called in to the police station during this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, four or five times, approximately. On four days I had to go to the police station around 9.00 a.m., and they would release me around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were -- at this time were there Muslim police officers or Muslim military officers present in your village or in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There were Muslims who worked, and Croats as well, who still worked, who were not disarmed, those who signed the act of loyalty. Others were, by that time, sent to camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you were arrested by the police, and if so, do you recall the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested and taken to the camp on the 23rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Those days, which were quiet, I had turned to my farming. Hay needed to be gathered, sowing needed to be done. When I came back home, I bought some hay, and I was taking care of my animals, making haystacks, and around 9.00 or 10.00 or 11.00, policemen perhaps came with a TAM vehicle, a covered truck carrying about two tonnes. They told me to get dressed and come with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They took us to the Ljubija police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you either while you were being transported or while you were at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you know a person by the name of Jovo Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him when you arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No -- yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Jovo Radocaj doing when you arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Jovo Radocaj was in the hallway hanging by his handcuffs on the bannister, by his right hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were at the police station, did you see anyone do anything to Jovo Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At that moment, the newly appointed policeman Miso Grbic arrived, who said, "You've been in this position, Jovo, since yesterday. Let's change your position." And he hung him from the bannister by his left arm, and he turned him in such a way that we couldn't see him any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, could the witness explain what he means when he said that he was hung from the bannister by his left arm? Does this mean that he was suspended in air?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe for us how Jovo Radocaj was handcuffed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 to the stairwell when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, at the level of the sixth or the seventh step, and the height is not an average man's height, yet he couldn't quite stand on the floor. He could touch the floor if standing on tiptoe, but he was suspended by his arm. He was stretched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, how did you know Jovo Radocaj from before the time you saw him at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him very well, ever since my youth, because he was an apprentice blacksmith, and he worked as an apprentice for [redacted] [redacted]. Later we worked for the same company, in the same department of that company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Jovo Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any idea or any information as to why Jovo Radocaj was in the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Allegedly, and that's what we heard at the camp when we arrived there, he was a member of the SDA party, which sounds incredible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDA party being the Bosniak political party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were Bosniaks. It was the Free Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, were you then taken from the police station in Ljubija to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- who was taken with you from the police station to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: In the van, we were about eight or nine men. Most of them were my acquaintances from Donja Ljubija. There was an Albanian whom I didn't know and there was Jovo Radocaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date and the approximate time that you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That was the 23rd of June, 1992, in the afternoon, sometime between 4.00 and 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe for us what happened to the group of people that you were with upon your arrival at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Savo Pusac, as the commander of the Ljubija police, was escorting us. He handed some papers to the guards at the weigh hut at the gate of the Keraterm camp. Then we got out of the van, lined up. And then Savo Pusac said, "Here I brought you one Serb, Jovo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Jovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. First, Mr. Kajin -- whether that is his last name or his nickname, I don't know -- hit him on the head so hard that he fell to the ground. Then another two or three guards joined him and kicked Jovo who was lying on the ground by the weigh hut. That lasted for about five, ten minutes, and then they showed Jovo to Room 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is to the interpretation. The witness said that not that he was hit in the head.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are looking right now for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another thing, the witness said after this, he sat on the ground not fell. He was actually given a rap or a crack on the head. Perhaps the witness should clarify for us what a rap or a crack on the head is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, would you seek a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please demonstrate for the Court what you saw the person you described as Mr. Kajin do to Jovo Radocaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I will try. It's not a rap like this. It's like this on the forehead with a middle finger which, for a man 60 years old, exhausted, who hadn't eaten for days, fell on the ground. He sat on the ground which, in his case, was the same as falling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you previously said hit or the word that you used, you really meant flick him with your finger; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. This usage of the word "crack" in our language is diverse. This is perhaps difficult to interpret into English, and this is why the misunderstanding may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, upon your arrival and after this incident with Jovo Radocaj, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We were sent to Room 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Court the conditions in Room 4 when you arrived there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Room 4 is the last in that Keraterm camp. It was somehow divided by a hallway in the middle. It was long. It went up to the middle of the room after which the room was shaped like a horseshoe. I was in the second part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately how high the ceiling was in Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, approximately three, three and a half, maybe four metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in Room 4 when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There were approximately 450, maybe 500 people. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you have to sleep on in Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Before our time, inmates were allowed to bring in wooden pallets which they lined one next to another, and onto them they piled clothing and that's where they slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after you first arrived in Keraterm, how long was it before you were given any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the food that you did receive during the time that you were at Keraterm, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: On the 24th of June, we got fed for the first time around 3.00 p.m. Some vehicle carrying food arrived. The food was distributed in front of Room 2. There was a sequence, a timetable for rooms to get food. We got two tiny slices of bread and some sort of soup very watery. Not really like soup, like salted water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the type of food that you received on most days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were there ever days when you were in Keraterm when you weren't fed at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: While I was there, 12 days, Room 3 was left without lunch. There was not enough food for all rooms, and one room was left out. It was Room number 2 or Room 3, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the overall camp conditions briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Generally, they were awful. They were impossible. It doesn't fall within the range of normal at all. As I said, we slept on those wooden pallets. We were 300, 400, 500 people, depending on the room. There was one toilet to which we could go in a file. Five men were released during the day, and they had to come back from the toilet within five minutes. The food was very poor and given out only once in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did there come a time while you were in Keraterm that you later saw Jovo Radocaj being mistreated in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you either saw or heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The first day, that was the 23rd of June in the evening, after the guards changed shift, Kajin and the guards which belonged to his shift, went home at around 6.00 or 7.00. I don't know when exactly they changed. And the shift that came in their stead included two brothers by the name of Banovic. In the evening when it was already quite dark, and since it was the summer, it may have been 10.00, 10.30 or 11.00 p.m., we heard some sort of shouting, commotion. Jovo Radocaj apparently was taken out from his room. We heard moans, cursing, insults. Things like, "You Serb joining the SDA. You should be skinned like a sheep for Bajram." That's a Muslim holiday. And during this beating, this group arrived somehow before our door, the door of Room number 4. We heard terrible moaning, screams of pain, and suddenly everything went quiet. The door of Room number 4 was opened and Mr. Jovo Radocaj was thrown into our room. Since I was sitting right next to the door, on a wooden crate, a crate for soda bottles, I wasn't able to sleep, and an acquaintance of mine was sitting next to me, we made room for Jovo Radocaj to lie down between us. He was covered with blood, terribly beaten up, black and blue. He was in a terrible state, asking for water, saying, "Please let me lie down. Give me water." And from 4.30 to 5.15, during that period he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what was done with Jovo Radocaj's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When it dawned, a different shift came. They changed around 7.00 or 6.00 in the morning and 7.00 or 6.00 in the evening, and then Jovo Radocaj's body and another one or two bodies were loaded onto a trolly in front of our room, and those corpses were taken somewhere behind the building and thrown onto some kind of waste dump.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you were in Keraterm that you saw Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Tokmadzic lay in that same hallway. He was the first next to the room, and I was first next to the door. It was a line of about 12 to 14 people. And on my first day, I spoke to Drago Tokmadzic. That was on the 23rd, in the afternoon. And on the 24th in the morning, we went to lunch together. That was on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Drago Tokmadzic later that day, and if so, please tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The next day, in the evening, that is the 24th, around the same time, Drago Tokmadzic was called out and he did come out. He was ordered to undress, to take off his top, whatever he had on him. I think it was a shirt or T-shirt. And then we heard the sound of blunt blows, which we could hear very well through the door. We couldn't see anything, but we could hear well. We heard cursing also. And from the moment when we started counting those blunt blows, I counted around 180 blows with brief breaks when they poured water over him to get him to come round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the people that were doing the beating saying anything to Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Something was being said regarding some car accident, some child who had been run over. This is what I heard. These voices punctuated by screams and moans, and something in reference to the Serb was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Drago Tokmadzic say anything or utter any words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He just kept moaning. He had no strength to say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards call anyone else out of the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The guards asked Drago whether there were other police officers with him in the room, and Drago mentioned the name of Esad Islamovic as he was losing his strength. And then Esad Islamovic was called out. And Esad Islamovic came out, and they -- again blows started and then moans Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 and screams of pain. That went on for another 20 minutes to half an hour. Then it quieted down, and then an order came that four men come out carry back those two in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask to go into closed session for just a few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after he was brought back into the room, can you describe what happened to Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Drago Tokmadzic was all black and blue. In other words, he was stripped to the waist. His trousers were wet. He had a Seiko watch which they had not taken, but it had been broken. Just the strap was there and the dial and the hands had fallen out. Drago Tokmadzic was unconscious. About 15 minutes to half an hour later, Drago died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what happened to Drago Tokmadzic's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Drago Tokmadzic's body lay there until the morning, and in the morning it was carried on the same cart that Jovo Radocaj was loaded on -- had been loaded on, and it was taken behind Room 4 somewhere, that Keraterm ceramics plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall a time when guards called out Albanian persons from the Keraterm -- from the rooms in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that incident for us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: First, one Albanian man was called out by name. I don't know who it was, I don't recall, but then it was ordered that all Albanians come out. Then all Albanians who were -- who were in our room - I think three or four were in our room - they were all taken out and again the same shouts and blows, the same blunt hits as with Mr. Jovo and with Tokmadzic. A couple of hours later, they were thrown back in. They all had injuries on their heads, arms. One of the Albanians was carried inside, into my room, and he remained there. He stayed there for six or seven days and then he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his condition during the six or seven days that he remained in your room prior to dying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Throughout this time, he was throwing up blood and something yellow or green. I don't know what it was, spleen or something. I think that all -- that everything inside, the internal organs were ripped and so he was dying for six to seven days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you know who that person was, this Albanian man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think you had ever seen him before? Do you recall ever seeing him before you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This Albanian arrived with us in the van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you ever seen him before that day in the van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a person by the name of Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kapetanovic was called out after the Albanian. It was the fourth night or the fifth night, and they called out his name. I don't know his first name, but it was Kapetanovic. He was a well-known person in town. I think he was a manager of a company. He was taken out and beaten up, and then was taken back to the room with a visible injuries but not life threatening, and he survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what ethnicity Mr. Kapetanovic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the Albanian people that were called out of the room, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There is no foundation for this question at all. The witness has testified he didn't know him. He only saw him in the van and being transported. And I think judicial notice could be taken that there are Albanians who are Catholics, orthodox and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it of importance what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how many days did you stay in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: 12 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you left Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. This was between 3rd and 4rd of July when we were ordered to make a list, the inhabitants of my village. We were told that we would be taken to the -- our stadium. We compiled a list, put our names down, and then two buses arrived. Then we boarded the buses. The -- those who escorted us were the special police unit members with red berets, blue uniforms, and they escorted us first onto the buses and then onward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, let me attempt to clarify, you were told that you were going to the stadium in Ljubija but, in fact, you were taken to Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what happened once the buses arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When we arrived in Omarska, we got off the buses, lined up, then they made a list of us again. Then we were put in a garage, a very small garage and we were 105. So we spent some time in that garage. Then they divided us into two groups. One group numbered 40, 45 and that group was sent to a small room above the hangar, and the other group remained in the garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how soon was it after your arrival in Omarska that you received anything to eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Court the conditions in the Omarska camp, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The conditions in Omarska were even more awful than those in Keraterm. Simply put, we had -- we didn't even have the pallets and blankets. We slept on the concrete. At night, we would sleep in the kitchen. And this last group that arrived during the day, we spent on the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the food and access to water in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We used industrial water that -- that was used by the mining company, and the food was distributed once every 24 hours. In this case, a loaf would be shared into eight equal parts so we could get one eighth of an 800 gram loaf. And on the plate, it would be .2 litres of -- we could call it a stew or a soup with some maybe vegetable or potato in it but no taste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there a person in the Omarska camp that you came to call the Karate Kid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. It was not myself who started call him Karate Kid but he, himself, while he was beating prisoners, he referred to himself as the Karate Kid. He would say, "I'm a Karate Kid, and now you'll see what it means to get beaten."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this person known as the Karate Kid mistreat any detainees in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what you saw him do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When we arrived on the 4th, between 4th and 5th of July, that night, it was Krkan's shift in which Karate Kid worked, and a gentleman called Safet Sumic was taken out of the room and -- he quickly returned with like a -- wearing a helmet, and he was told that he should collect -- should make a collection to take the money for all the damage done to the room like broken windows, broken lock, things like that. That was to be like 120.000 Serb dinars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when the Karate Kid mistreated you personally and, if so, can you please tell us about that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. First, he kicked me. I was in the room with these other fellow inmates. And the second time when the Karate Kid entered the room, he was looking -- he said, "Where's the money," because we had only collected about 5.000, 6.000 dinars. And then I dared say that all the money had been taken away from us at Keraterm because that is what had happened. Then he cursed my mother. He kicked me in the chest, around the heart. And that was very convenient to him, because I was sitting on the floor. It was a very hard kick so I nearly blacked out from this kick. He attempted to hit another fellow inmate in the head, but he avoided the kick and then he went out again and then he started -- and then we started being called out. I was called out fifth or sixth. I was taken to another room. There was only an office desk in it and there were -- there was the Karate Kid, and there were three additional guards and the fourth and a fifth guard was outside with his rifle cocked. Then questioning started. Did I answer call-up? And when I answered not, that I was not in a reserve force for that last year, then the question was why. Then again they asked for money, did I have any money. And then the beatings started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of instruments did they use to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The Karate Kid was to the right, and for the most part he was kicking me with his right foot, and he had either a military -- military boots or some hiking boots. I think that they were made in Slovenia. On the other side, there was another guy who was kicking me with his left foot on the front, and then another one was there with a police baton and another one with a piece of cable or something, and those two were beating me from behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what type of injuries did you receive as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I had -- both my eyebrows broken. I had swellings under my eyes, then in my kidney area. But during this beating, I was able to stay on my feet for about 15, 20 feet. Then after I fell down, they continued to kick me while I was lying. Then I crawled out all on my -- all fours out of the room. As I was doing that, other guards stopped me and asked me to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 make a three-finger salute. Then I got a severe blow with a piece of cable that had some kind of metal ending, and later on it turned out that I had a two- or three-centimetre long gash and a fracture at the base of my skull so that I suffer from severe headaches even to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that your eyebrows were broken. Can you please indicate what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were both cut from the blows that I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time shortly after this beating incident that you were called out of the room to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what happened on that day, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was taken to the room above the kitchen on that day. That was in the so-called administration building. That was the third or fourth room upstairs from the staircase, and I was interrogated there by some older gentleman who was somewhat greying. In my opinion, he was from Banja Luka. So he questioned me whether -- you know, what I was a part of, whom I knew. And when he did not get the answers that he wanted from me, he called in two guards. They were again members of the special units, in camouflage uniforms. They had a real military look, whereas the others really looked like ragtag soldiers. Then one hit me in one kidney, the other one in the other. Those were kicks with their boots. I started losing consciousness, but I was able to straighten up on my knees, and I said, "Whatever the gentleman heard from me is what I have to say, and you can kill me now." Then he waved to them. They stopped kicking me and I was allowed to go back to the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, were you familiar with any kind of classification scheme that was used on the basis of these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't know, but we ourselves identified certain categories. Whoever was sent to the "white house," that person was to be killed because they would not survive that. Whoever was sent to the pista, those were either -- to them or to us, they seemed like sort of lighter cases and they would hang on longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified about being out on the pista. Can you describe for the Court what the pista is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Pista was an area of -- which was paved with concrete, between the administration building on the one side and the big structure, the garage where they kept heavy machinery, the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the pista covered or was it open to the elements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It was open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you forced to stay on the pista?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I stayed on the pista for about 15 days during daytime. In the evening when it would get dark, we would be ordered to either go to the kitchen and the tables would be pushed off to the side and we were there in the middle, and the other one -- the other group would be taken to Rooms 26 and 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many people were with you out on the pista?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Five hundred, 600, 700 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move around on the pista?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. We had to lie there all day long, for the most part on our stomachs so we would not be able to see the mistreatment of our fellow inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were in Omarska, did you ever see any bodies, dead bodies, in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many dead bodies did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Approximately 13, 14, 15. I'm not sure about the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, while you were in Omarska, did you see any women being detained there, and if so, approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, women were also detained there. While we were on the pista during the day, women were in the kitchen. They were, for the most part, hanging around the window and watching us, observing us. There were between 25 and 40 of them there. I'm not sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you had seen any women being detained in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. The first couple of days, I saw two women in passing. I recognised one of them, one lady, and I -- I did not know the other one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how long did you remain in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Thirty-two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day did you leave and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: From what I remember, and it's not so easy years hence, it was on the 6th of August that names were called out and some men were taken to Trnopolje. I think there were 110 men per bus, and I think there were about 10, 11 buses, and we were bused to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the conditions like in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At Manjaca, we slept in a barn that was used for cattle. That was -- that was -- and then part of the floor was covered with macadam. We slept in three rows. Fortunately, I was in the middle, which was concrete, and that is where I slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, how long did you remain at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At Manjaca I stayed until 16 December 1992, when under auspices of UNHCR and ICRC we were freed and escorted to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of that escort process, did you have to sign any documents or take any oath or make any kind of promises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. We signed documents that we would not come back to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness I. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Witness I, we are now going to take a break for half an hour. During the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody including the members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned until 11.30. --- Break taken at 11.02 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Could we go please, very briefly, into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, I want just to very briefly explore the issues surrounding the call-ups which were issued in late 1991. Were those call-ups sent to all citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: All members of the reserve army in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it within your knowledge that similar call-ups were sent to reservists in other opstinas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a demonstration organised, was there not, against the call-ups? Did you participate in any way in the organisation of that demonstration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The first time when I was called up into the reserve force of the 5th Kozarac Brigade of the Prijedor municipality, that is the Territorial Defence of Prijedor. I responded. We were at Benkovac, that is in 1991 when the problems in Slovenia were taking place. The second time when I was called up in 1991 in October, it was already clear that it was necessary to go to the front line in Croatia. At that time, I took part in the demonstrations before the town hall in Prijedor. I boycotted the mobilisation and didn't respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness I. It's that demonstration that I was talking about. Did you take part in its organisation in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. It was a spontaneous gathering of all reservists, all the citizens who didn't want to go to Croatia to lose their lives for nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard, Witness I, from another witness who has told us about how it was an organised demonstration, but you say it was spontaneous, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I maintain it was spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that the majority of Croats and Muslims in your area declined to honour the call-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, the overwhelming majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, some Muslims and some Croats did go to the fighting in Croatia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As for those others, it's their own problem, and it is true that a small number of people did honour the call-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the plebiscite which was held in about February 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a plebiscite organised by, in large part, the SDS party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Not in large part but completely. What was indicated was that it was a plebiscite of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you, Witness I, is that it was not confined only to Serbs but that all other people could take part in it if they so chose. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, whoever felt as a Serb, anyone who wished to disregard their own religion or ethnicity. I don't know how many of them there could have been in Bosnia and Herzegovina, maybe a couple of cases, but what was indicated on the posters which were all around was a plebiscite of the Serbian people, whereas in the case of the referendum, it was all the referendum of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about that referendum. The people who did vote, there were both Muslims and Croats who did take part in the SDS-organised plebiscite, didn't they? 25 A. No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were of non-Serb origin who took part in it, Witness I, they had a perfect democratic right to take part in that expression of opinion, didn't they, if they so chose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of anyone from my municipality who took part in that plebiscite of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the ethnic make-up of your home district, Witness I. I'd just like to ask you a little bit more about the ethnic make-up of Yugoslavia. Would you accept this proposition, that prior to 1992, Serbs as a whole were in a majority throughout the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were Serbs living in every republic and autonomous region that existed in 1992, were there not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event that those republics and autonomous regions were to have broken away from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the effect would be, would it not, that the Serbs would have become a minority in every area except for what is now the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: With the separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the former Yugoslavia, Serbs would not become a minority but would have become a constituent part of Bosnia-Herzegovina's ethnic make-up because there are no minorities there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who regarded themselves as owing allegiance to the Serb Nation would have become in numbers a minority in not just Bosnia-Herzegovina but everywhere else except for what is now the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Is that right or not, Witness I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Sir, they are a minority if we look at the entire world or Europe. Someone somewhere has to be a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a relative straightforward question. Why not simply answer, "Yes," and go on? Let's not waste any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- going back to the second referendum which was held about which you spoke, that was boycotted by the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept, Witness I, that it was their democratic right not to take part in such a referendum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: What their right was, anyone could turn out at the referendum. It was free. One part of their people did take part in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now, please, to the period around February/March 1992, it's right, isn't it, that on both sides, people began to organise themselves for the protection of themselves and their families; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for example, buses were organised allowing people to travel where they wanted to out of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That would have been convenient for the Serbian Democratic Party if people had left of their own accord, then they would remain a majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if you'd like to answer the question now, please, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the things that were organised, Witness I, were buses which took people of whatever nationality out of the region of Prijedor; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, mostly women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were people of all ethnicities; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't on any of the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see what you told the Office of the Prosecutor when you made a long, 31-page statement to them in 1994 was this: "At this time, buses from the Prijedor bus company were travelling to Belgrade and Banja Luka and Serbs were able to travel to these places and get out of Prijedor." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition, there were Muslims going to Zagreb and other places, were there not, in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the takeover of power in Prijedor had taken place, there was initially no effect whatever on your home area of Donja Ljubija, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDA remained in power in your village, did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how soon after the takeover of power in Prijedor was a Crisis Staff formed in Donja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the Crisis Staff in Ljubija was established, but it was about a month and a half or two later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- how was the Crisis Staff formed, by appointment, by election, what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The people of my village gathered in the cinema hall and they elected somehow about 10 people on to that Crisis Staff so that they could talk to the newly-established representative body of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we briefly go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Crisis Staff was set up, is it right that people in the village also voted to take up arms, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not vote that you were going to take steps to defend yourselves in the event of any form of military activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It was agreed only that we would not sign the act of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Office of the Prosecutor in 1994 this: "We voted that we were going to defend ourselves if we were attacked." Do you recall saying that, Witness I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. If we voted as we did, that we wouldn't sign the oath of loyalty, then we had to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff took charge of the police in Donja Ljubija, did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, that is what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in 1994. It's right, isn't it, that the structure of the police remained exactly as it had been before the takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was decided, was it not, that civilians were going to man checkpoints alongside those very same police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't at any time wear any sort of uniform or insignia whilst doing that, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those civilians who were manning checkpoints were armed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Hunting weapons changed hands. They were shared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as an incident at Hambarine on 21st of May, 1992 is concerned, it's right, isn't it, that you were aware that a number of occupants, Serb occupants, of a motor vehicle were fired upon and wounded during such an incident at a checkpoint? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't know about it. I found out later, at the end. And it says also in the statement that reservists from the vehicle fired first and that provoked a response to their fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recall your statement. Have you read it recently, Witness I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, please, to the issue of an ultimatum on the 24th of May, 1992, to the Crisis Staff. It's right, isn't it, that the surrender having effectively taken place, the Serb authorities were obviously satisfied with how and what had taken place in your village? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the consequence of that were that no shots were fired at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of Muslims and Croats elected to remain in the police force at that time. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You perceived those people as traitors, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man Jovo Radocaj, who was thought -- was a Serb and was thought to have voted for the SDA, the Serbs thought of him as a traitor, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, about this: The police chief was a man called Branko Bjekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, for a while. After that, he was taken to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was, by ethnicity, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. He was commander of the police after the takeover of the police force in Ljubija, but only formally, on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then two Croats, also members of the police, Drincic -- one called Niko Drincic and another, his son Darko Drincic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both those men took part in detentions of people in the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. They were real traitors. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as late as December 1994, Darko Drincic was still working for the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then a man -- I'm going to ask you now about some Muslims who continued to work for the police. Mujo Odobasic. Do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Avdo Topic, was he a Muslim policeman who continued to work after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was in the reserve force of the police, and he continued working after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fikret Brdar or Brda, was he a Muslim who continued to work in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. All of them continued on the police force for a while. After we were taken to the camp, all of them, to the last man, were discharged, their uniforms and weapons were taken away, and they were taken to the camp, some of them. Others were killed in front of their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence force continued to exist, did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Which Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor was this: "The Territorial Defence forces became known as the Serbian Territorial Defence forces." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of those who took part in the so-called Serbian Territorial Defence forces non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think that they were also some of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this be correct, Witness I, that Bosnians of Muslim ethnicity and Bosnian of Croat ethnicity at that time considered they had allegiance to the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side of that particular coin, the Serbs who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina considered that they had allegiance to Serbia, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I didn't consider it. They were loyal to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an occasion, was there not, when a Serb military unit came into the area and began to misbehave, some by looting and some by other forms of misbehaviour; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, is it not, that the Serb police stopped their activities the morning after they had arrived; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. After they had covered that is crossed over to the mid-point in the village, when they had covered more than half of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was at around this time when 500 men from Donja Ljubija were rounded up and taken to the football stadium. It's right, isn't it, that they were allowed to go home as a result of the intervention of the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a problem with a particular military unit called the 5th Kozara Brigade of the Territorial Defence of Prijedor in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. At about this time, was there a particular problem with a unit known as the 5th Kozara Brigade of the Territorial Defence from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it those that the Serbian police were engaged in trying to control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't recall whether that was the 5th Kozara Brigade, but I know that there were all kinds of uniforms. But it wasn't a brigade, it was a mob. It was a large group of armed people who went about looting in my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were detained and taken to Keraterm, you were interrogated several times, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I wasn't interrogated. I just had to be present at the police station and then they would let me go in the afternoon, and the next morning I would have to report myself. So I would come and go on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to the manner of the interrogations in a moment, Witness I. It's right, isn't it, that amongst those who were interrogating you were Drago Tokmadzic, a Croat; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. From what I recall, Drago Tokmadzic was from a mixed marriage so he was half Croat, half Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another man called Mirko Daljevic; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, indeed, asked a number of questions, were you not, Witness I, at that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, about your political affiliations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: All questions boiled down to the situation, the tension, and obviously it included political ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your view of that interrogation was that it was a mild and not unpleasant interrogation; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were interrogated again by the same two men; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, on another occasion when I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had by now acquired some form of uniform, had you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I had not acquired any kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they not question you about a uniform which you had made yourself, Witness I, a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I did make one myself, but I said that I was not issued one. But, yes, I did have one made on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you confirm that it was a camouflage uniform that you had made for yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That was done from canvas used for tents that was more like some kind of a poncho that would protect one from the rain and the elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right isn't that the chief of police came and spoke to you about that uniform and advised you to be careful of what you were doing, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Bjekic said, Branko Bjekic. And he, himself, was already at risk. He knew what was in the offer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an occasion after these two interrogations, was there not, when you were detained by the head of the Territorial Defence, Slobodan Taranjac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was interested in whether or not you belonged to an organisation known as the green berets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said you weren't, he released you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that release, you were summoned several times to the police station but not interrogated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about that time, it's right, is it not, that the days remained quiet and the people were able to go about their business as they had always been doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, except that I could not go to work at that time, because I was spending all days in the police station. My child was hungry and wet all day long. My mother, his grandmother, was unable to help him because he was -- she was ill. My wife was in the hospital. I did not know where she was and what was going on with her. And this is what you call quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if I may just remind you briefly so that we can refresh your memory as to what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor: "For me it was quiet. For me it was quite. The days were quiet and people were able to go to the fields and do their work." Do you recall saying that to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Except for the days when I was at the police station, and quiet was in the sense of not -- there not being any shooting, and this was a sort of lull before a storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, you refer to "people." That, I suggest, is the inhabitants of Donja Ljubija, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, you were actually gathering hay at the time when you were arrested? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
